title: Training Mechanics: Full FT, Adapters, Mixed Precision, Checkpointing & GPU Memory
scopeHtml: Scope: Full fine-tuning, adapters, mixed precision, gradient checkpointing and estimating training memory.

notes.title: What lives in GPU memory during training
notes.html:
Before any technique makes sense, you need a picture of what actually fills a GPU while a model trains. A GPU (graphics processing unit) is the chip that does the matrix maths; it has its own fast memory called VRAM (video RAM, for example 24 GB on a consumer card, 80 GB on an A100 or H100). If your training job needs more bytes than the VRAM holds, you get the dreaded CUDA out of memory error and the job dies. Almost every trick in this note exists to avoid that error.

A parameter (also called a weight) is one learned number inside the model. A "7B model" has about 7 billion of them. Training is a loop: run the model forward on some text to get a prediction, measure the error (the loss), run backward to find how each parameter should change (the gradient), and let an optimizer nudge the parameters. Each of those steps keeps different data alive in VRAM. There are exactly four buckets:

GPU memory during one training step
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. WEIGHTS          the model itself            (N params) |
| 2. GRADIENTS        one number per trainable param         |
| 3. OPTIMIZER STATE  Adam keeps 2 extra numbers per param   |
| 4. ACTIVATIONS      intermediate results of the forward    |
|                     pass, kept so backward can use them    |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
 1+2+3 scale with model size N.   4 scales with batch x sequence length.
 (plus small stuff: logits, CUDA context, fragmentation)

Why does backward need activations? Backpropagation uses the chain rule. To compute how a layer's weights should change, it needs the layer's input from the forward pass. So the forward pass stores those inputs (the activations), and backward consumes them. This is why training needs several times more memory than inference: inference only needs bucket 1 (plus a small cache), training needs all four.

Each technique in this note attacks one bucket:

Technique Bucket it attacks
Mixed precision (bf16/fp16) weights, gradients, activations: fewer bytes each
Adapters / LoRA gradients and optimizer state (only a tiny part is trainable)
Gradient checkpointing activations (recompute instead of store)
8-bit optimizers, ZeRO/FSDP sharding optimizer state, gradients, weights (spread or shrink)

Real products: every open-weight fine-tune you have seen (Llama, Mistral, Qwen derivatives on Hugging Face) was made by combining several of these. The peft, transformers, bitsandbytes, DeepSpeed and PyTorch FSDP libraries are the tools. Hosted fine-tuning APIs (OpenAI, Google Vertex, Together, Fireworks) hide all of this from you but pay the same memory bill internally, which is part of why they charge per training token.

Everyday analogy, placed after the explanation: a GPU is a workbench of fixed size. The model is the machine bolted to it, gradients and optimizer state are the tools and notes you keep beside it, and activations are the half-finished parts you must keep within reach until the next stage needs them. When the bench is full, you either get a bigger bench, shrink the parts, or put some parts in a box and rebuild them later.

See also: C6/notes/02_P1.md section "Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient" gives the 16 bytes per parameter headline; this note derives it and goes into the mechanism.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "a 7B model needs 14 GB to train". 14 GB is the bf16 weights only; training needs weights plus gradients plus optimizer state plus activations.
  • Forgetting activations. They are the only bucket you control by batch size and sequence length, and they often cause the OOM, not the weights.
  • Mixing up inference and training memory. Inference has no gradients, no optimizer state and no stored activations (it keeps a KV cache instead).

notes.title: Full fine-tuning: updating every parameter
notes.html:
What it is. Full fine-tuning (FFT) continues training a pretrained model on your data and lets gradient descent change every single weight. If the model has 7 billion parameters, 7 billion numbers can move. A pretrained model is one that already learned language from a huge corpus; fine-tuning teaches it a narrower behaviour (your tone, your format, your domain) with a much smaller dataset.

Why it exists. It gives the most capacity to change. If your task needs the model to learn a new language, a new domain's vocabulary (continued pretraining on medical or legal text), or a big behavioural shift, touching every weight gives the most room.

How it works, step by step.

for each batch of tokenised text:
  1. forward : tokens -> embeddings -> N transformer layers -> logits
               (store activations as you go)
  2. loss    : cross-entropy between logits and the true next tokens
               (usually only on the assistant/answer tokens)
  3. backward: chain rule layer by layer from the loss to the input,
               produce a gradient for EVERY parameter
  4. step    : AdamW reads gradient + its two running averages,
               writes new weights
  5. zero the gradients, next batch

Step 4 is where Adam's cost hides. AdamW (the default optimizer for LLMs) keeps two running numbers per parameter: m, a moving average of the gradient (the "momentum"), and v, a moving average of the squared gradient (used to scale the step per parameter). Those two numbers per parameter are the optimizer state, and they are usually stored in 32-bit floating point for numerical safety.

Pros. Highest ceiling on quality for large distribution shifts; no extra inference machinery (you ship a new checkpoint); works for continued pretraining.

Cons. Expensive (we compute how expensive in the next sections); one full model copy per task (a 7B bf16 checkpoint is about 14 GB on disk per variant); catastrophic forgetting (the model gets good at your data and loses general ability because all weights drifted); harder to roll back; easy to overfit on small data. See also C6/notes/01_W1.md for when fine-tuning is worth it at all.

Typical hyperparameters (verify for your model). Learning rates for full fine-tuning are small, often in the range 1e-6 to 2e-5, with a warm-up (a few percent of steps ramping from zero) and cosine or linear decay; 1 to 3 epochs. Too high a learning rate on all weights is the classic way to wreck a pretrained model.

Code: the core training step (GPU training code is Python-only in practice).

# Minimal full fine-tuning loop with Hugging Face + PyTorch.
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

name = "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B"          # example id, verify access/licence
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16).cuda()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-5, weight_decay=0.01)

batch = tok(["Q: 2+2?\nA: 4"], return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
out = model(**batch, labels=batch["input_ids"])   # forward + loss
out.loss.backward()                                # gradients for ALL params
opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()                        # Adam updates every weight
print(out.loss.item())                             # prints the scalar loss
// No sensible Kotlin snippet: full fine-tuning needs CUDA tensors, autograd and
// an optimizer (PyTorch/JAX). The JVM has no mainstream GPU training stack for LLMs.
// A JVM service would call a trained model, or launch the Python job:
val job = ProcessBuilder("python", "train_sft.py", "--config", "full_ft.yaml")
    .inheritIO().start()          // runs the Python trainer, streams its logs
println("exit=" + job.waitFor())  // prints 0 on success
// Same reason as Kotlin: no practical JVM LLM training stack.
// A Java orchestrator (batch job, CI step) just starts the Python trainer.
Process job = new ProcessBuilder("python", "train_sft.py", "--config", "full_ft.yaml")
        .inheritIO().start();               // runs the Python trainer
System.out.println("exit=" + job.waitFor()); // prints 0 on success

Real systems that used full fine-tuning: the instruction-tuned and chat versions of open models (for example Llama-2-Chat and Alpaca-style recipes started with supervised full fine-tuning), and domain models such as BloombergGPT-style continued pretraining (verify specifics in each paper).

Analogy, after the explanation: full fine-tuning is repainting and rewiring the entire house to suit a new owner. You can change anything, but it costs a lot, takes long, and you might accidentally remove something useful.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming full fine-tuning always beats LoRA. On many instruction-style tasks the gap is small; "better" depends on data size and how far the target is from pretraining.
  • Using a pretraining-sized learning rate (1e-3) for fine-tuning; it destroys the model within a few steps.
  • Forgetting that fine-tuning for a narrow task can reduce general ability (forgetting), so you must keep a general eval alongside the task eval.

notes.title: GPU memory calculations: the 16 bytes per parameter rule
notes.html:
What it is. A back-of-the-envelope method to estimate, before you rent a GPU, whether a training run will fit. You do arithmetic on bytes per parameter, then add an activation estimate.

Why it exists. GPUs are expensive and out-of-memory errors waste hours. Estimating first lets you choose hardware, batch size and technique (LoRA vs full, checkpointing or not).

Bytes per number format.

Format Bytes Notes
fp32 (float32) 4 the "full precision" default
fp16 / bf16 2 half precision
fp8 1 newer hardware (verify)
int8 1 quantized
4-bit (NF4) 0.5 QLoRA base weights

Step 1: the weights. Memory = parameters x bytes per parameter. For N = 7e9:

  • fp32: 7e9 x 4 = 28e9 bytes = 28 GB (using 1 GB = 1e9 bytes for simplicity; in GiB it is about 26).
  • bf16: 7e9 x 2 = 14 GB.

Step 2: the standard mixed-precision AdamW recipe (the one in the ZeRO paper and in most trainers). Per parameter you store:

bf16 weights (used in forward/backward)      2 bytes
bf16 gradients                                2 bytes
fp32 master copy of the weights               4 bytes
fp32 Adam m (momentum)                        4 bytes
fp32 Adam v (squared-gradient average)        4 bytes
----------------------------------------------------
total                                        16 bytes per parameter

The ZeRO paper writes this as 2 + 2 + K bytes, with K = 12 for Adam. So for 7e9 parameters: 7e9 x 16 = 112e9 bytes = 112 GB. That is already more than one 80 GB H100, before a single activation. For a 70B model: 70e9 x 16 = 1,120 GB, about 1.1 TB, which must be sharded across many GPUs.

Variants worth knowing (all derived the same way):

  • Pure fp32 training: 4 (weights) + 4 (grads) + 8 (Adam) = 16 bytes. Same total, no speed benefit.
  • bf16 weights with no master copy, Adam states in fp32: 2 + 2 + 8 = 12 bytes, so 84 GB for 7B. Smaller, but pure-bf16 updates lose small steps (see the mixed precision section).
  • 8-bit Adam (bitsandbytes): 2 + 2 + 4 + 2 (two 1-byte states) = 10 bytes, so 70 GB for 7B.
  • Plain SGD with momentum: one state instead of two. Rarely used for LLMs.

Step 3: activations. This depends on batch size b, sequence length s, hidden size h, layers L and attention heads a. A widely cited estimate from Korthikanti et al. (2022, "Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models") for 16-bit training without any recompute is, per layer:

activation bytes per layer  ~=  s * b * h * (34 + 5 * a * s / h)

The 5*a*s/h term comes from the attention score matrices (size s x s per head). Worked example, a Llama-7B-like shape: h = 4096, L = 32, a = 32, s = 2048, b = 1.

s*b*h              = 2048 * 1 * 4096              = 8,388,608
5*a*s/h            = 5 * 32 * 2048 / 4096         = 80
per layer          = 8,388,608 * (34 + 80)        = 956,301,312  ~ 0.96 GB
all 32 layers      = 0.956 GB * 32                ~ 30.6 GB   (per sequence!)

With FlashAttention (which never materialises the s x s matrix) the 80 term disappears: 8,388,608 x 34 x 32 = 9.1 GB. With batch size 4 multiply by 4. This is why a "7B fits on my card" belief collapses at long sequence length: activations grow linearly with b and s, and the attention term grows with s squared when it is not fused.

Step 4: the small stuff. The logits tensor is b x s x vocab x 4 bytes (fp32 for the loss): 1 x 2048 x 32,000 x 4 = 262 MB for a 32k vocabulary; for a 128k vocabulary (Llama-3-style) that is about 1.05 GB, and softmax/loss copies can double it. Add the CUDA context (roughly 0.5 to 1 GB), temporary buffers and allocator fragmentation; budget 10 to 20 percent headroom (a rule of thumb, measure it).

Putting it together for 7B full fine-tuning, b = 1, s = 2048, FlashAttention, no checkpointing: 112 GB (states) + 9.1 GB (activations) + ~1 GB (logits) + overhead is about 125 GB. Does not fit on one 80 GB GPU; needs sharding (next sections) or a different method.

Code: a calculator you can keep in a repo.

def train_mem_gb(n_params, bytes_w=2, bytes_g=2, bytes_master=4, bytes_adam=8,
                 trainable_frac=1.0):
    """Static memory in GB (1e9 bytes): weights + grads + master + Adam.
    Frozen params only pay for weights. Activations are NOT included."""
    frozen = n_params * (1 - trainable_frac)
    train = n_params * trainable_frac
    total = n_params * bytes_w + train * (bytes_g + bytes_master + bytes_adam)
    return total / 1e9

def act_gb(s, b, h, layers, heads, flash=True, ckpt=False):
    """Korthikanti et al. estimate for 16-bit activations."""
    per_layer = s * b * h * (34 + (0 if flash else 5 * heads * s / h))
    if ckpt:                       # keep only each layer input (2 bytes), + 1 layer live
        return (2 * s * b * h * layers + per_layer) / 1e9
    return per_layer * layers / 1e9

print(round(train_mem_gb(7e9), 1))                     # 112.0
print(round(act_gb(2048, 1, 4096, 32, 32, flash=False), 1))  # 30.6
print(round(act_gb(2048, 1, 4096, 32, 32, ckpt=True), 2))    # 0.54+0.29 = 0.83
// Same arithmetic on the JVM (useful in a capacity-planning service or CI check).
fun trainMemGb(nParams: Double, bw: Int = 2, bg: Int = 2, bMaster: Int = 4,
               bAdam: Int = 8, trainableFrac: Double = 1.0): Double {
    val train = nParams * trainableFrac
    return (nParams * bw + train * (bg + bMaster + bAdam)) / 1e9
}

fun actGb(s: Int, b: Int, h: Int, layers: Int, heads: Int, flash: Boolean = true): Double {
    val attn = if (flash) 0.0 else 5.0 * heads * s / h
    return s.toDouble() * b * h * (34 + attn) * layers / 1e9
}

fun main() {
    println(trainMemGb(7e9))                       // 112.0
    println(actGb(2048, 1, 4096, 32, 32, false))   // about 30.6
}
// Plain-math estimator; no libraries needed.
public final class TrainMem {
    static double trainMemGb(double n, int bw, int bg, int bMaster, int bAdam, double frac) {
        double train = n * frac;
        return (n * bw + train * (bg + bMaster + bAdam)) / 1e9;
    }
    static double actGb(int s, int b, int h, int layers, int heads, boolean flash) {
        double attn = flash ? 0.0 : 5.0 * heads * s / h;
        return (double) s * b * h * (34 + attn) * layers / 1e9;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(trainMemGb(7e9, 2, 2, 4, 8, 1.0));   // 112.0
        System.out.println(actGb(2048, 1, 4096, 32, 32, false)); // about 30.6
    }
}

To measure instead of estimate (Python only): call torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() after a few steps, and torch.cuda.memory_summary() to see what is holding memory. Estimates are for planning; measurements are for decisions.

Analogy, after the explanation: it is like estimating the luggage for a trip. Each traveller (parameter) needs a suitcase (weights) plus a toiletry bag (gradient) plus two notebooks (Adam). Multiply by the number of travellers, then add the souvenirs you pick up on the way (activations) and a margin for things you forgot.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting "4 bytes per parameter" or "2 bytes per parameter" as the training cost. The mixed-precision AdamW answer is 16 bytes per parameter for trainable parameters.
  • Giving a memory number without stating the sequence length and batch size; activation memory is meaningless without them.
  • Forgetting the fp32 master weights, which are the usual missing 4 bytes.
  • Ignoring the vocabulary: with a 128k vocab the logits alone can cost over a gigabyte at long sequence lengths.

notes.title: Mixed precision: fewer bytes per number, faster maths
notes.html:
What it is. Mixed precision training does most arithmetic in 16-bit floats (fp16 or bf16) while keeping a few critical things (master weights, optimizer state, loss accumulation) in 32-bit. The idea comes from Micikevicius et al. 2017, "Mixed Precision Training" (NVIDIA and Baidu).

Why it exists. Two reasons. Memory: 16-bit tensors take half the bytes, which halves activations and communication. Speed: modern GPU tensor cores (specialised matrix units, present from NVIDIA Volta onward) run 16-bit matrix multiplies many times faster than fp32 (the exact ratio depends on the GPU; verify on the vendor spec sheet).

Floating point in plain words. A float stores a sign, an exponent (how big, the range) and a mantissa (the precision, the number of significant digits).

Format Exponent bits Mantissa bits Max value Resolution near 1.0
fp32 8 23 ~3.4e38 ~1.2e-7
fp16 5 10 65,504 2^-10, about 0.001
bf16 8 7 ~3.4e38 2^-7, about 0.0078

fp16 vs bf16. fp16 has more precision but a tiny range: it overflows above 65,504 and underflows (rounds to zero) for very small gradients, below roughly 6e-8 (the smallest subnormal). bf16 ("brain float", from Google) keeps fp32's range with fewer mantissa bits, so it almost never over/underflows. That is why bf16 is the default on Ampere (A100) and newer GPUs and on TPUs. fp16 remains necessary on older GPUs (V100, T4) that lack bf16.

Loss scaling (needed for fp16). Gradients are often tiny; in fp16 they would round to zero. So you multiply the loss by a large factor S (for example 65,536) before backward, which scales all gradients by S, then divide gradients by S before the optimizer step. If a gradient comes out as inf or NaN (overflow), skip that step and halve S; after many good steps, grow S again. This is dynamic loss scaling, implemented by PyTorch GradScaler. bf16 does not need it.

Why master weights in fp32. Suppose a weight is 1.0 and the update is lr x grad = 1e-4. In bf16, the spacing between numbers near 1.0 is 2^-7 = 0.0078, so 1.0 + 0.0001 rounds back to 1.0: the update vanishes. In fp32 near 1.0 the spacing is about 1.2e-7, so the update survives. The fp32 master copy accumulates tiny updates faithfully; the bf16 copy is just re-derived from it for the next forward pass. This is the 4 bytes you saw in the 16-byte recipe. Pure-bf16 training without master weights is possible (and saves 4 bytes per parameter) but needs tricks such as stochastic rounding or Kahan summation; plain pure-bf16 with tiny learning rates silently stalls.

What stays in fp32 under autocast. Operations sensitive to range or accumulation (softmax, layer norm, loss, reductions) are run in fp32 automatically by PyTorch's autocast; matrix multiplies and convolutions run in 16-bit. You do not choose per op; autocast has a built-in list.

Mixed-precision step (bf16)
 fp32 master weights --cast--> bf16 weights --forward--> activations (bf16)
                                                  |
 fp32 Adam update  <--cast-- bf16 gradients <-- backward
 (writes new fp32 master weights)

FP8 and beyond. H100-class GPUs and Transformer Engine support fp8 matmuls for even more speed; it is newer and framework specific (verify current support before relying on it). TF32 is a different thing: an Ampere+ matmul mode that keeps fp32 storage but reduces mantissa inside the tensor core.

Code.

import torch
from torch.amp import autocast, GradScaler

model, opt = build_model().cuda(), None            # build_model() is yours
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-5)

# bf16 (A100/H100/RTX30+): autocast only, no scaler needed
for batch in loader:
    with autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        loss = model(**batch).loss                  # matmuls in bf16, softmax/LN in fp32
    loss.backward()
    opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()

# fp16 (V100/T4): add dynamic loss scaling
scaler = GradScaler("cuda")
for batch in loader:
    with autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16):
        loss = model(**batch).loss
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()                   # scaled gradients
    scaler.step(opt); scaler.update()               # unscale, skip if inf/NaN, adjust S
    opt.zero_grad()

# With Hugging Face Trainer it is one flag:
#   TrainingArguments(bf16=True)   # or fp16=True on older GPUs
// No sensible Kotlin snippet for autocast (it is a PyTorch runtime feature).
// What a JVM developer CAN usefully do is reproduce the rounding argument:
fun main() {
    val w = 1.0f; val update = 1e-4f
    println(w + update)        // 1.0001 in float32: the update survives
    // bf16 keeps 7 mantissa bits: spacing near 1.0 is 2^-7 = 0.0078125,
    // so 1.0 + 0.0001 would round back to 1.0 (update lost). That is why
    // master weights stay in fp32.
}
// No Java autocast either. Same demonstration of why master weights are fp32:
public class Rounding {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        float w = 1.0f, update = 1e-4f;
        System.out.println(w + update);       // 1.0001 in float32
        // bf16 spacing near 1.0 is 2^-7 = 0.0078125, so the same add rounds to 1.0.
        System.out.println(Math.ulp(1.0f));   // 1.1920929E-7 : fp32 spacing near 1.0
    }
}

Real products. Almost every large model since BERT-era training uses mixed precision: GPT-3-class models trained in fp16 with loss scaling, while PaLM, Llama and most newer models train in bf16 (verify per paper). Frameworks: PyTorch AMP, NVIDIA Apex (legacy), Hugging Face Accelerate/Trainer, DeepSpeed.

Production failure patterns.

  • Loss becomes NaN a few hundred steps in with fp16: loss scale too aggressive, an overflow in attention logits, or a learning rate too high. Fixes: bf16, lower lr, gradient clipping (norm 1.0), check for bad data rows.
  • Loss does not decrease with pure bf16 and a tiny learning rate: updates being rounded away; use fp32 master weights.
  • "bf16 is on but memory is the same": the model was loaded in fp32 and autocast only casts per-op, so weights still cost 4 bytes. Load with torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 if you intend bf16 weights and fp32 master states.
  • Evaluating a bf16-trained model in fp16 can overflow; keep the same dtype family.

Analogy, after the explanation: mixed precision is doing your rough sketching on a small notepad (fast, cheap) but keeping the official ledger in a big, precise book. If you wrote every tiny correction only on the notepad, small amounts would smudge out.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying bf16 is "more precise" than fp16. It has a larger range but less precision (7 vs 10 mantissa bits).
  • Claiming mixed precision halves total training memory. The 16-byte recipe is the same size as fp32 training for weights+states; the savings are mainly in activations and speed.
  • Using loss scaling with bf16 (unneeded) or forgetting it with fp16 (gradients underflow).
  • Forgetting that some ops (softmax, norm, loss) must remain in fp32.

notes.title: Gradient checkpointing: trade compute for memory
notes.html:
What it is. Instead of storing every layer's activations for the whole forward pass, store only a few checkpoints and recompute the missing ones during backward. You pay extra compute and save a large amount of activation memory. Also called activation checkpointing or rematerialisation. The classic reference is Chen et al. 2016, "Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost".

Why it exists. From the memory section, activations for a 7B model at 2048 tokens were about 30.6 GB per sequence (9.1 GB with FlashAttention). That number grows with batch and sequence length and is often what actually triggers OOM. Gradient checkpointing breaks that linear growth.

How it works, step by step.

Without checkpointing (store everything)
 L1 -> L2 -> L3 -> L4 -> L5 -> L6 -> loss
 keep A1 A2 A3 A4 A5 A6           memory ~ L layers of activations

With checkpointing at every layer (what HF does by default)
 Forward : run L1..L6, keep ONLY each layer's INPUT; drop the insides
 Backward: reaching L6, re-run L6's forward from its saved input to
           rebuild its activations, then backprop through it, free them,
           move to L5, repeat
 memory  ~ L inputs + ONE layer's full activations at a time

Numbers (Llama-7B-like, s = 2048, b = 1, from the earlier section). Each layer's input is s x b x h x 2 bytes = 2048 x 4096 x 2 = 16.8 MB; 32 layers keep 0.54 GB. Add one layer's full activations being rebuilt: 0.29 GB with FlashAttention (34 x 8,388,608 = 285 MB). Total about 0.83 GB versus 9.1 GB (flash) or 30.6 GB (no flash). That is roughly a 10x reduction.

The cost. You run the forward pass of each checkpointed layer a second time. A training step is roughly forward (1 unit) + backward (about 2 units) = 3 units; adding a recompute of the forward makes it 4 units, so about 33 percent more compute in the worst case. In practice teams report roughly 20 to 35 percent slower steps (measure, it depends on the kernels). If you checkpoint only some layers (selective recompute, as in Korthikanti et al. who recompute only the cheap-but-large attention parts), you recover most of the memory saving for a smaller cost.

Classic theory. With n layers and checkpoints every sqrt(n) layers, memory drops from O(n) to O(sqrt(n)) with one extra forward pass. LLM frameworks usually checkpoint per transformer block, which is simpler and good enough.

Gotchas.

  • Randomness: dropout must produce the same mask when recomputed. PyTorch's checkpoint saves/restores the RNG state by default.
  • Non-reentrant vs reentrant: PyTorch's torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint(fn, x, use_reentrant=False) is the recommended mode (verify in current docs); the older reentrant mode needs at least one input requiring grad, which bites with frozen embeddings.
  • LoRA plus checkpointing: the input embeddings are frozen so no input requires grad; call model.enable_input_require_grads() (peft) or use non-reentrant mode, otherwise gradients silently do not flow and the adapter does not learn.
  • use_cache=True (the KV cache) conflicts with checkpointing; Hugging Face warns and disables it. Set model.config.use_cache = False for training.
  • BatchNorm-style layers with running statistics would update twice; transformers use LayerNorm/RMSNorm so this rarely matters.

Code.

# Hugging Face: one line
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()           # per-block checkpointing
model.config.use_cache = False                  # KV cache off during training
# With peft/LoRA also:
model.enable_input_require_grads()

# Or in TrainingArguments:
#   TrainingArguments(gradient_checkpointing=True, bf16=True, ...)

# Raw PyTorch on your own block:
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint
class Net(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        for blk in self.blocks:
            x = checkpoint(blk, x, use_reentrant=False)  # recompute blk in backward
        return x
// No sensible Kotlin snippet: checkpointing is an autograd feature inside PyTorch.
// The JVM-side value is the budget calculation (matches the numbers above):
fun ckptActGb(s: Int, b: Int, h: Int, layers: Int): Double {
    val kept = 2.0 * s * b * h * layers      // one fp16 input per layer
    val oneLayer = 34.0 * s * b * h          // one layer rebuilt (FlashAttention)
    return (kept + oneLayer) / 1e9
}
fun main() = println(ckptActGb(2048, 1, 4096, 32))   // about 0.83
// No Java checkpointing API either; here is the same budget helper.
public class Ckpt {
    static double ckptActGb(int s, int b, int h, int layers) {
        double kept = 2.0 * s * b * h * layers;   // layer inputs, 2 bytes each
        double oneLayer = 34.0 * s * b * h;       // one layer rebuilt (FlashAttention)
        return (kept + oneLayer) / 1e9;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(ckptActGb(2048, 1, 4096, 32)); // about 0.83
    }
}

Real products and tools. Hugging Face Transformers/Trainer (gradient_checkpointing), DeepSpeed activation checkpointing, Megatron-LM selective recomputation, PyTorch FSDP + apply_activation_checkpointing, Unsloth (advertises its own optimised checkpointing; verify claims). Nearly every public QLoRA recipe turns it on.

Production failure patterns.

  • Training is 30 percent slower than expected after turning it on: that is the recompute cost, not a bug. Only keep it on if you cannot fit the batch otherwise; a bigger batch can offset the slowdown by better GPU utilisation.
  • The adapter loss stays flat only when checkpointing is on: the enable_input_require_grads problem above.
  • Warnings that use_cache is incompatible: harmless, but set it explicitly so logs are clean.
  • Memory still high: weights/optimizer state are not reduced by checkpointing; it only helps activations.

Analogy, after the explanation: studying for an exam by writing only chapter summaries instead of full notes. When you need details of one chapter you re-read the book for just that chapter, which takes extra time but your backpack stays light.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying it reduces weights or optimizer memory; it only reduces activation memory.
  • Quoting "2x slower"; the usual figure is about one extra forward pass, about 20 to 35 percent per step.
  • Forgetting it is incompatible with use_cache=True and the frozen-embedding gradient issue in LoRA.
  • Confusing it with gradient accumulation (which splits a batch over steps to save activation memory without recompute).

notes.title: Adapters: train a small add-on instead of the whole model
notes.html:
What it is. Adapters are small trainable modules added to a frozen pretrained model. You train only the adapter parameters (often 0.1 to 2 percent of the total) and leave the original weights untouched. This family is called parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). The word "adapter" is used in two senses: the original bottleneck adapter layers, and (loosely) any add-on such as LoRA weights. We cover both.

Why it exists. Full fine-tuning copies the whole model per task and needs 16 bytes per parameter. If you freeze the base model, gradients and optimizer state are needed only for the tiny adapter, and you ship a few megabytes per task instead of tens of gigabytes. One base model can then serve many customers or tasks by swapping adapters.

Bottleneck adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019). Insert after the attention and feed-forward sublayers of each transformer block a small network: project the hidden vector of size d down to a small size m, apply a nonlinearity, project back up to d, and add the result to the original through a residual connection (output = input + adapter(input)). Initialise the up-projection near zero so at the start the model behaves exactly like the original.

hidden (d=4096)
   |-----------------------+   residual path (identity)
   v                       |
 down-project d -> m (64)  |
 nonlinearity (GELU/ReLU)  |
 up-project   m -> d       |
   v                       |
   +--------- add <--------+
   v
 hidden (d=4096)

Parameter count per adapter: 2 x d x m + m + d (two weight matrices plus biases). For d = 4096, m = 64: 2 x 4096 x 64 = 524,288, plus 4,160 for biases = about 528k. Houlsby places two per layer, 32 layers: about 33.8M trainable parameters, roughly 0.5 percent of a 7B model. The downside: adapters add extra sequential layers, so inference gets a little slower (latency and no way to fold them into the weights), which is the main reason LoRA overtook them for LLMs.

LoRA (Hu et al., 2021). Add a low-rank update to an existing weight matrix: y = Wx + (alpha / r) x B(Ax), where A is r x k, B is d x r and r is small (for example 8 or 16). B starts at zero. Trainable parameters per matrix: r x (d + k). Because the update is a plain matrix addition, you can merge it: W' = W + (alpha / r) x BA, giving zero extra inference cost.

Count for a Llama-7B-like model, r = 16, all linear projections:

  • q, k, v, o: each 4096 x 4096, so 16 x (4096 + 4096) = 131,072 each; times 4 = 524,288.
  • gate, up, down: each between 4096 and 11008, so 16 x (4096 + 11008) = 241,664 each; times 3 = 724,992.
  • Per layer: 524,288 + 724,992 = 1,249,280. Times 32 layers = 39,976,960, about 40M, which is 40M / 6.74B = about 0.6 percent (Llama-7B has about 6.74B parameters).

Memory for LoRA training of that model, bf16 frozen base plus fp32 adapter states: base weights 6.74e9 x 2 = 13.5 GB; adapter 40M x (4 weights + 4 grads + 8 Adam) = 40M x 16 = 0.64 GB; activations as before (shrunk with checkpointing). Compare 112 GB for full fine-tuning: the static cost drops about 8x. See also C6/notes/02_P1.md section "LoRA" for hyperparameter guidance (rank, alpha, target modules, learning rate).

QLoRA. Quantize the frozen base to 4-bit NF4 so weights cost about 0.5 bytes per parameter: 6.74e9 x 0.5 = 3.4 GB (a bit more with quantization constants). Then 7B fine-tuning fits comfortably on a 12 to 16 GB card; the 70B fits on a single 48 GB card as quoted in the QLoRA paper (verify exact figures). See also C6/notes/02_P1.md section "QLoRA".

Other adapter-style methods.

  • Prefix tuning / prompt tuning / P-tuning: learn a few "virtual token" vectors prepended to the input (prompt tuning) or to every layer's attention keys/values (prefix tuning). Tiny parameter counts, usually weaker on small models.
  • (IA)3 (Liu et al., 2022): learn per-channel scaling vectors that multiply keys, values and the feed-forward activations; roughly 0.01 percent of parameters.
  • BitFit: train only the bias terms.
  • DoRA, LoRA+, rsLoRA, AdaLoRA and others: refinements of LoRA (verify current status in the peft docs).

Code.

# Hugging Face peft: attach LoRA adapters to a frozen model
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)   # example id
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
                 target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj",
                                 "gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"])
model = get_peft_model(base, cfg)
model.print_trainable_parameters()   # prints trainable params vs total, about 0.5-0.7%

# After training: save only the adapter (MBs), or merge for serving
model.save_pretrained("out/adapter")
merged = model.merge_and_unload()    # W' = W + BA, no inference overhead
// Training adapters is Python-only. A realistic Kotlin/JVM role: parameter math
// and serving. Count LoRA parameters for a planning tool:
fun loraParams(r: Int, dims: List<Pair<Int, Int>>, layers: Int): Long =
    dims.sumOf { (d, k) -> r.toLong() * (d + k) } * layers

fun main() {
    val dims = listOf(4096 to 4096, 4096 to 4096, 4096 to 4096, 4096 to 4096, // q k v o
                      4096 to 11008, 4096 to 11008, 4096 to 11008)            // gate up down
    println(loraParams(16, dims, 32))   // 39976960
}
// Java: same planning math. (Serving adapters is done by vLLM/TGI, not the JVM.)
import java.util.List;
public class LoraCount {
    record Dim(int d, int k) {}
    static long loraParams(int r, List<Dim> dims, int layers) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (Dim m : dims) sum += (long) r * (m.d() + m.k());
        return sum * layers;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        List<Dim> dims = List.of(new Dim(4096,4096), new Dim(4096,4096),
            new Dim(4096,4096), new Dim(4096,4096),
            new Dim(4096,11008), new Dim(4096,11008), new Dim(4096,11008));
        System.out.println(loraParams(16, dims, 32)); // 39976960
    }
}

Real products and tools. Hugging Face peft (LoRA, IA3, prefix tuning), AdapterHub (bottleneck adapters, Pfeiffer and Houlsby configs), vLLM and S-LoRA (serving many LoRA adapters on one base model), LoRAX (Predibase), Unsloth, Axolotl, TRL. Apple's on-device foundation model and Google's Gemini Nano both ship a base model plus small task adapters on device (verify the current details in each vendor's docs), an example of the "one base, many adapters" idea reaching phones; relevant for Android developers.

Production failure patterns.

  • Adapter trained on a base model version, then loaded onto a different revision or a differently quantized base: outputs degrade silently. Store the base model id and revision with the adapter.
  • Merging a LoRA into a 4-bit quantized base gives rounding damage; merge into a 16-bit copy then re-quantize and re-evaluate.
  • Rank too low for a task that needs new knowledge: loss plateaus; raising rank or targeting MLP layers often helps more than extra epochs.
  • Forgetting target_modules: peft picks defaults for some architectures only; an unknown architecture raises an error or trains almost nothing. Check the trainable parameter count printed.

Analogy, after the explanation: adapters are like clip-on lenses for a camera. The expensive main lens (base model) stays the same and untouched, and you carry a handful of small clip-on lenses (adapters) for different shots, swapping them as needed.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying adapters train "no extra memory"; they still need gradients and optimizer state for their own parameters, and activations still flow through the full frozen model.
  • Believing LoRA saves activation memory. It does not; backprop still goes through the frozen layers, so you still need gradient checkpointing for long sequences.
  • Mixing up bottleneck adapters (extra layers, inference overhead) with LoRA (mergeable, no overhead).
  • Assuming LoRA always matches full fine-tuning; on tasks that demand new knowledge or large shifts, it can fall short.

notes.title: Worked example: will it fit on my GPU?
notes.html:
Now combine everything into one decision, the way you would in an interview or a planning meeting. Model: a Llama-7B-like network with about 6.74B parameters (use 7e9 for the round numbers below), b = 4, s = 2048, FlashAttention, target card: one 24 GB GPU (for example an RTX 4090) or one 80 GB GPU (A100/H100).

Plan Weights Grads + optimizer Activations Total Fits 24 GB? Fits 80 GB?
Full FT, bf16 + AdamW fp32, no ckpt 14 98 (14 grads, 28 master, 56 Adam) 4 x 9.1 = 36.4 ~148 no no
Full FT, 8-bit Adam + ckpt 14 14 grads + 28 master + 14 states = 56 4 x 0.83 = 3.3 ~73 no tight (yes with small margin; measure)
LoRA r=16, bf16 base, ckpt 14 0.64 3.3 ~18 borderline (OOM risk with logits and overhead) yes
QLoRA 4-bit base, ckpt 3.5 0.64 3.3 ~7.5 yes yes, with room for b > 4

How to read the arithmetic: Full FT states = 7e9 x (2 grad + 4 master + 8 Adam) = 98 GB, plus 14 GB of weights = 112 GB (the 16 bytes per parameter). The first row adds activations 4 x 9.1 = 36.4 GB giving about 148 GB. Row 2 swaps Adam's 8 bytes for 2 bytes (8-bit) so states = 7e9 x (2 + 4 + 2) = 56 GB. Rows 3 and 4 are mostly dominated by the frozen weights.

Sharding when a single GPU is not enough. If you must do full fine-tuning of 7B or larger, split the 16 bytes across GPUs. ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al., 2020, DeepSpeed) has three stages: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also the parameters. With N GPUs and stage 3, per-GPU static memory is roughly 16 x params / N. Example: 7e9 x 16 / 8 GPUs = 14 GB per GPU for states (plus activations and communication buffers). PyTorch FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) implements the same idea natively. Offloading to CPU RAM or NVMe (ZeRO-Offload / ZeRO-Infinity) trades speed for capacity.

Code: measure, do not guess.

import torch
torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
for i, batch in enumerate(loader):
    loss = model(**batch).loss
    loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
    if i == 3: break
peak = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
print(f"peak allocated: {peak:.1f} GB")      # allocated tensors; reserved is higher
print(torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved() / 1e9) # what the caching allocator holds
// JVM planning helper: pick the first plan that fits with 15% headroom.
data class Plan(val name: String, val gb: Double)

fun firstFit(plans: List<Plan>, gpuGb: Double): String? =
    plans.firstOrNull { it.gb * 1.15 <= gpuGb }?.name

fun main() {
    val plans = listOf(Plan("full-ft", 148.0), Plan("full-8bit-ckpt", 73.0),
                       Plan("lora-ckpt", 18.0), Plan("qlora-ckpt", 7.5))
    println(firstFit(plans, 24.0))   // lora-ckpt is 20.7 with headroom, fits: prints lora-ckpt
    println(firstFit(plans, 80.0))   // full-8bit-ckpt is 84 with headroom: prints lora-ckpt
}
// Same helper in Java.
import java.util.List;
public class FirstFit {
    record Plan(String name, double gb) {}
    static String firstFit(List<Plan> plans, double gpuGb) {
        for (Plan p : plans) if (p.gb() * 1.15 <= gpuGb) return p.name();
        return null;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        List<Plan> plans = List.of(new Plan("full-ft",148), new Plan("full-8bit-ckpt",73),
            new Plan("lora-ckpt",18), new Plan("qlora-ckpt",7.5));
        System.out.println(firstFit(plans, 24)); // lora-ckpt
        System.out.println(firstFit(plans, 80)); // lora-ckpt (73 x 1.15 = 84 > 80)
    }
}

Note the headroom check is why the 80 GB card does not pick the 73 GB plan: 73 x 1.15 = 83.95 GB, above 80. Real runs vary; treat this as a first filter, then measure.

Analogy, after the explanation: choosing a van for a house move. Full fine-tuning is renting the biggest truck; LoRA is a van; QLoRA is a car with the furniture vacuum-packed. You count boxes first, then pick the vehicle, rather than discovering at the loading dock that the sofa will not fit.

Common interview traps.

  • Producing one number without stating assumptions (dtype, optimizer, batch, sequence, checkpointing, FlashAttention).
  • Applying ZeRO stage 3's "divide by N" to activations; sharding does not shrink activations (data parallel replicas each hold their own).
  • Treating nvidia-smi memory as the model's need; PyTorch's caching allocator reserves more than it uses, so use max_memory_allocated.
  • Forgetting that increasing context length (not just batch) multiplies activation memory.

notes.title: Other memory levers worth knowing
notes.html:
These are smaller than the big four but come up constantly in interviews and in real jobs.

Gradient accumulation. Instead of one batch of 32 sequences, run 8 micro-batches of 4, add up their gradients, and take one optimizer step. Same effective batch (32), activation memory of batch 4. Cost: no extra compute, just more steps per update. Pitfall: loss normalisation. If you average the loss per micro-batch and sequences have different numbers of tokens, you weigh tokens unevenly; modern trainers have fixed this, so verify your version.

8-bit and paged optimizers. bitsandbytes offers AdamW8bit and paged variants that keep the optimizer states in 8 bits (a block-wise quantization), cutting Adam from 8 to about 2 bytes per parameter, and paging spikes to CPU RAM. Quality is usually close to 32-bit Adam (verify on your task).

FlashAttention. Computes attention in tiles without writing the full s x s score matrix to memory, removing the quadratic activation term. It is an exact algorithm (not an approximation), it is also faster, and recent PyTorch builds expose it via scaled_dot_product_attention (verify the backend selection).

Sequence packing and length bucketing. Padding wastes memory and compute. Packing several short examples into one 2048-token row (with attention masks so they do not see each other) raises token throughput; sorting by length reduces padding.

Smaller vocabulary head / chunked loss. The logits tensor can be large; some trainers (Liger kernels, Unsloth) compute the loss in chunks, avoiding materialising the full b x s x V fp32 tensor (verify the library claims).

Freezing layers. A cheap partial fine-tune: freeze embeddings and the lower half, train the top layers. Saves gradients and optimizer states for the frozen part; a simple middle ground, though LoRA is usually better quality per byte.

Code.

from transformers import TrainingArguments
args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="out",
    per_device_train_batch_size=2,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=16,     # effective batch 32 per device
    bf16=True,
    gradient_checkpointing=True,
    optim="paged_adamw_8bit",           # bitsandbytes paged 8-bit AdamW (verify name in your version)
    learning_rate=2e-4,                 # LoRA-range lr; use ~1e-5 for full FT
    max_grad_norm=1.0,                  # gradient clipping against spikes
    warmup_ratio=0.03,
    lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
)
print(args.gradient_accumulation_steps * args.per_device_train_batch_size)  # 32
// Config-as-code check on the JVM side, e.g. a validator for a training request:
data class TrainCfg(val microBatch: Int, val accum: Int, val gpus: Int) {
    val effectiveBatch get() = microBatch * accum * gpus
}
fun main() = println(TrainCfg(2, 16, 1).effectiveBatch)   // 32
// Same effective-batch formula in Java.
public class EffBatch {
    static int effective(int micro, int accum, int gpus) { return micro * accum * gpus; }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(effective(2, 16, 1)); // 32
    }
}

Analogy, after the explanation: gradient accumulation is carrying 32 bricks to a wall in 8 trips of 4 because you cannot hold 32 at once; the wall ends up the same, you just walk more.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing gradient accumulation and gradient checkpointing are the same; one splits the batch, the other recomputes activations.
  • Saying FlashAttention is an approximation. It is exact; it changes memory access, not the maths.
  • Using an adaptive-optimizer learning rate from a LoRA recipe (2e-4) on a full fine-tune; full FT needs 10x to 100x smaller.
  • Thinking effective batch size is only per-device batch; multiply by accumulation and number of GPUs.

notes.title: Production failure patterns and debugging
notes.html:
Training problems are mostly memory, numerical, or data issues. A working checklist:

1. Out of memory at step 0 vs at step 800. At step 0: weights + states + activations simply do not fit; apply the table above. At step 800: usually a longer-than-average batch (sequence length spike), or memory fragmentation. Fix by capping max_seq_length, sorting/packing, or setting PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True (verify the option for your PyTorch version) to reduce fragmentation.

2. Out of memory only at evaluation or generation. Eval runs without checkpointing and may use larger batches or a KV cache. Lower the eval batch size; wrap eval in torch.no_grad().

3. OOM when saving a checkpoint. Gathering a sharded model (FSDP/ZeRO-3) to rank 0 can double memory. Use sharded checkpoints and a separate consolidation step.

4. NaN or exploding loss. Check for: fp16 without loss scaling, a learning rate that is too high, a bad row (empty target, extremely long text), or divide-by-zero in a custom loss when every token is masked. Enable gradient clipping (1.0), switch to bf16, log the gradient norm.

5. Loss goes down but outputs are poor. Not a memory problem: wrong chat template, loss computed on prompt tokens, duplicated data, or evaluating a different tokenizer. See also C6/notes/01_W1.md section "Data formats and pitfalls".

6. The adapter is not learning. Check the printed trainable parameter count; with checkpointing check enable_input_require_grads; make sure the optimizer was created after get_peft_model; make sure you did not load the base with requires_grad=False on the adapter by mistake.

7. Throughput is much lower than expected. Possible causes: data loader bottleneck (tokenising on the fly with one worker), padding waste, checkpointing on when memory was fine, CPU offload enabled, communication-bound multi-GPU setup, or an fp32 matmul path (forgot bf16/TF32). Look at GPU utilisation and tokens per second per GPU.

8. Cost surprises. Cloud GPU hours dominate. Rule of thumb for compute: training FLOPs are about 6 x parameters x tokens (forward 2 + backward 4). For 7e9 parameters and 1e9 training tokens: 6 x 7e9 x 1e9 = 4.2e19 FLOPs. If a GPU sustains an effective 150e12 FLOP/s (an illustrative figure for a well-utilised A100-class card in bf16, verify for your hardware), that is 4.2e19 / 1.5e14 = 280,000 seconds, about 78 GPU-hours. With gradient checkpointing add roughly one third. For LoRA the backward pass skips the weight-gradient computation for frozen weights, so the cost is somewhat lower than 6N (but activations gradients still flow); treat 6N as the upper bound.

Code: a training-time guardrail.

import torch
def check_step(model, loss, max_norm=1.0):
    if not torch.isfinite(loss):
        raise RuntimeError("non-finite loss: check lr, dtype, data row")
    gn = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm)  # returns pre-clip norm
    if gn > 100:
        print("warning: grad norm spike", float(gn))
    return float(gn)
# call after loss.backward() and before opt.step()
// A JVM service that watches training logs can apply the same rule to the metrics stream.
fun isHealthy(loss: Double, gradNorm: Double): Boolean =
    loss.isFinite() && gradNorm < 100.0
fun main() {
    println(isHealthy(2.31, 0.8))          // true
    println(isHealthy(Double.NaN, 0.8))    // false
}
// Same health check for a log-watching job.
public class Health {
    static boolean healthy(double loss, double gradNorm) {
        return Double.isFinite(loss) && gradNorm < 100.0;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(healthy(2.31, 0.8));         // true
        System.out.println(healthy(Double.NaN, 0.8));   // false
    }
}

Analogy, after the explanation: debugging training is like troubleshooting a car that will not start. Check fuel (memory), the spark (numerics), and the driver (data) in order, rather than replacing the engine.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to "buy a bigger GPU" before checking sequence length, padding and checkpointing.
  • Treating a NaN loss as a hardware problem; it is almost always dtype, learning rate or data.
  • Quoting "6 x N x tokens" FLOPs for LoRA without noting it is an upper bound.
  • Ignoring that eval and checkpoint saving have their own memory peaks.

notes.title: How the techniques stack: a decision guide
notes.html:
Pulling the pieces together into a sequence you can follow and defend.

Step 1: decide the method. Does prompting or RAG already solve it? If not, start with LoRA or QLoRA. Move to full fine-tuning only when evals show a persistent quality gap that a higher rank and more target modules cannot close, or when doing continued pretraining on a large domain corpus.

Step 2: pick the precision. bf16 if the GPU supports it (A100, H100, RTX 30/40 series, TPUs); fp16 with loss scaling on older cards; fp32 master weights and Adam states in almost all cases.

Step 3: compute the static memory. 16 bytes per trainable parameter plus 2 bytes per frozen parameter (or 0.5 for QLoRA).

Step 4: add activations. Use the s x b x h x 34 x L estimate (FlashAttention) and compare to what is left. If it does not fit, enable gradient checkpointing first; then reduce micro-batch and use gradient accumulation.

Step 5: if still too big. 8-bit paged optimizers; ZeRO/FSDP sharding across several GPUs; CPU offload; a smaller sequence length; a smaller base model.

Step 6: measure. Run 5 steps, read max_memory_allocated, compare with your estimate, and record the ratio so your next estimate is better calibrated.

Decision flow
 Need to change model behaviour?
   -> try prompt / RAG first
   -> still no: LoRA (bf16 base)
        -> 4-bit base if VRAM is tight (QLoRA)
        -> quality gap persists? full FT (8-bit Adam, ZeRO/FSDP)
 Always: bf16 + FlashAttention
 OOM?  checkpointing -> smaller micro-batch + accumulation -> offload/shard

Real-world pattern. A typical open-source recipe for a 7B to 8B instruct fine-tune: QLoRA or bf16 LoRA, r = 16 to 64, all linear layers, learning rate around 1e-4 to 2e-4, bf16, gradient checkpointing, paged 8-bit AdamW, effective batch 16 to 64 via accumulation, 1 to 3 epochs, on one 24 to 80 GB GPU. A typical full fine-tune of a 70B model: 16 to 64 H100 GPUs with FSDP or ZeRO-3, bf16, checkpointing, learning rate around 1e-5 (verify against the model's published recipe).

Code: the recipe as one config.

from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import TrainingArguments, BitsAndBytesConfig
import torch

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
                         bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16)   # QLoRA base
lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
                  target_modules="all-linear")                    # verify option in your peft version
args = TrainingArguments("out", per_device_train_batch_size=2,
                         gradient_accumulation_steps=16, bf16=True,
                         gradient_checkpointing=True, optim="paged_adamw_8bit",
                         learning_rate=2e-4, num_train_epochs=2)
# Load model with quantization_config=bnb, call prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model),
# then get_peft_model(model, lora), then Trainer/SFTTrainer(model, args, ...).
print(args.learning_rate)   # 0.0002
// Kotlin: the same recipe as a typed config object a backend could submit to a
// training service (the trainer itself runs in Python).
data class FineTuneRequest(
    val method: String = "qlora", val rank: Int = 16, val alpha: Int = 32,
    val bf16: Boolean = true, val checkpointing: Boolean = true,
    val microBatch: Int = 2, val accumSteps: Int = 16, val lr: Double = 2e-4,
    val epochs: Int = 2)
fun main() = println(FineTuneRequest())   // prints the data class with all defaults
// Java: record version of the same request (Java 16+).
public class Recipe {
    record FineTuneRequest(String method, int rank, int alpha, boolean bf16,
                           boolean checkpointing, int microBatch, int accumSteps,
                           double lr, int epochs) {}
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(new FineTuneRequest("qlora", 16, 32, true, true, 2, 16, 2e-4, 2));
    }
}

Analogy, after the explanation: it is a packing list for a trek. Pick the lightest tent that does the job (LoRA), vacuum-pack the clothes (4-bit, bf16), leave the bulky items at base and rebuild them when needed (checkpointing), and only hire a mule train (many GPUs) when you truly must carry a whole house.

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending full fine-tuning by default; a senior answer starts with the cheapest approach that meets the eval bar.
  • Listing techniques without ordering them or stating which memory bucket each addresses.
  • Forgetting to re-evaluate after merging or quantizing an adapter.
  • Not mentioning measurement; every estimate should be validated with a short real run.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Training memory has four buckets: weights, gradients, optimizer state, activations. Inference needs only weights (plus a KV cache), which is why training costs several times more.
  • Full fine-tuning updates every parameter. With mixed-precision AdamW it costs about 16 bytes per parameter (2 bf16 weights + 2 grads + 4 fp32 master + 8 Adam), so 7B needs about 112 GB before activations; 70B needs about 1.1 TB.
  • Activations scale with batch x sequence length; a per-layer estimate is s x b x h x (34 + 5 a s / h) bytes in 16-bit, and FlashAttention removes the quadratic term. Work the arithmetic with stated assumptions.
  • Mixed precision computes in bf16 or fp16 and keeps fp32 master weights and Adam states. bf16 has fp32's range with less precision and needs no loss scaling; fp16 needs dynamic loss scaling. Master weights exist because small updates vanish in 16-bit.
  • Gradient checkpointing saves only layer inputs and recomputes the rest during backward: about 10x less activation memory for about one extra forward pass (roughly 20 to 35 percent slower steps). It does nothing for weights or optimizer state.
  • Adapters freeze the base and train a small add-on. Bottleneck adapters add layers; LoRA adds a mergeable low-rank update with r x (d + k) parameters per matrix (about 40M, 0.6 percent, for r = 16 on a 7B model). QLoRA adds a 4-bit frozen base so 7B fits on a consumer GPU. LoRA does not reduce activation memory.
  • Other levers: gradient accumulation (different from checkpointing), 8-bit paged optimizers, FlashAttention, ZeRO/FSDP sharding, packing.
  • Failure patterns: OOM at step 0 vs later, NaN loss from dtype or learning rate, adapters not learning with checkpointing (enable_input_require_grads), peak memory at eval or save time, and throughput lost to padding or offload.
  • Method: choose the cheapest approach that meets the eval bar, compute static memory, add activations, apply levers in order, then measure with max_memory_allocated.
  • Mark as "verify" before relying on them: exact API option names in your transformers/peft/bitsandbytes versions, tensor-core speed ratios, and FP8 support.
